submission.natural_language_explanation: The positive pole is a retrospective detector for the linking ' of' and/or the head token of a stock two-noun 'X of Y' compound term in its bare form (no determiner after 'of'): it fires strongest on quality of life (peaks 10-13 at both ' of' and ' Life'), then end of life, bill of materials, terms of service, quality of service, cost of living, depth of field and field of vision (4-10 at the peak), and quality of care and point of view (3-6), while the words alone are inert (' service' reads 0.6 alone but 8.5 in 'terms of service'). Membership is lexical, not semantic or frequency-driven: substituting a merely similar domain noun keeps only the weak ' of' response (quality of education 1.6-3.8 vs 10.4), and compositional of-phrases of other shapes stay at the floor (place of birth 0.1-0.9, state of the art 0.2-0.7, speed of light 0.3-0.6, cause of death 1.3-2.4); reordering ('life quality', 'service terms') kills the peak, a determiner after 'of' roughly halves it (quality of the life 4.0 vs 10.4), the hyphenated/glued spellings are the same feature and fire as strongly or stronger (quality-of-life 13.5, ease-of-development 10.0, time-of-flight 7.6, out-of-the-box 6.4, internetofthings 3.5), and arbitrary initialisms mostly stay at the floor (only the scanned stored strings fire: SIL OFL, R.O.C., BOD, BioFOG, nOTScale, POV).

Halloween is a day that the children in particular wait for with much anticipation and for good reason, for the day means a time of lots of fun and excitement. But what if it was made a completely new experience by going eco-friendly? Our garages are a storehouse of discarded and disposable items. Why not make use of our imagination and ingenuity to create some Halloween day objects out of them. Here let us have a look at some innovative ways by which you can create your own Halloween crafts-
Hardware Halloween Pumpkin
To this Halloween mascot, you can add lots and loads of your creativity by decorating it with a variety of discarded junk items like screws, pins, and nuts, washels and bolts, and create amazingly attractive facial features like nose, ears, eyes and mouth.
Net bag spider webs
You can create spider webs for Halloween by simply cutting out pieces from discarded net bags or by cutting out a web from a trash bag.
Recycled water bottle ghosts
Simply cut away the neck part of the bottle. Glue cheesecloth on the inverted side of the bottle that will serve as the top end of the ghost figures. Drape this cloth around the bottles sufficiently long to lend it a spooky look. Then cut out pieces of paper in fancy colors to create eyes, nose and mouth for the figures. Stick them on and the recycled water bottle ghost is ready. You can even light it up to make it look even spookier.
Make bat costume for the kids from the broken umbrellas lying around in your house. Just detach the cloth (with the metal spikes intact) from the stick. These spikes will make ribs of the bat wings. Cut the umbrella cloth right in middle. Just stick the two pieces on the clothes your kid is wearing on the underarm side to create bat wings.
Cd made Jack o’ lantern
Take a few old discarded CDs and etch out facial expressions on. Suspend them from the ceiling or simply from your doorway with the help of strings.
Plastic milk jug lanterns
Just cut the bottom of the jugs and draw out some weird facial features on them with crayons or sketch pens. Place white light bulbs underneath, switch them on and enjoy the ghostly spectacle of white light illuminates them.
Paper mache puppets
Prepare paper Mache glue by boiling three parts of flour in four parts of water. Let the mixture cool. Take an inflated tiny balloon. Glue strips of paper on it to create a bulbous structure roughly matching a human head. Keep aside and let the bulb dry. Then pierce in a hole on the underside of this bulb to puncture the balloon.
Insert a stick from here into it and secure it with glue. Then paint the bulb in the color of your choice. Etch facial features on this bulb when the color dries up to make it look like a face. Cut out a cloth just enough to cover the length of the stick. Stitch it around the stick on the underside of the bulb in the form of a petticoat. Title: The Vineyard Crew

Act 1:

We open on a panoramic shot of the California countryside, with the sun setting on a beautiful vineyard. Cut to a group of five friends, GREG, a laid-back surfer type, MIMI, a high-strung perfectionist, HENRY, a charming ladies’ man, LUCY, a free-spirited artist, and JAY, a clumsy and naive amateur gardener.

The group is gathered around a table in the middle of the vineyard, drinking wine and admiring the grape vines. Greg has just revealed his idea to buy the vineyard and start their own business. Mimi is immediately excited about the idea, but the others are skeptical.

Jay: “I don’t know anything about growing grapes!”
Lucy: “I’ve never even tasted wine before!”
Henry: “I’m in as long as there’s plenty of women around.”

The group decides to give it a shot and dive in headfirst, despite their lack of experience.

Act 2:

The crew struggles with a variety of challenges as they attempt to start their vineyard. Mimi is constantly micromanaging everyone, trying to make everything perfect. Lucy accidentally runs over a few of the grape vines with her truck while trying to park it in the vineyard. Jay forgets to water the plants for a few days, and Henry spends more time flirting with customers than actually helping with the business.

Things reach a breaking point when the group realizes they’re about to miss a crucial deadline for the harvest. Everyone starts to panic, but Greg stays calm and thinks on his feet. He gathers the group together and comes up with a plan to get everything done in time. They all pitch in and work through the night to finish the harvest.

Act 3:

The group is exhausted but elated after completing the harvest on time. They celebrate with a big party in the vineyard, inviting all their friends and family. Mimi finally lets loose and has a few glasses of wine, while Lucy teaches everyone how to paint a picture of the vineyard.

All seems well until the group realizes they accidentally mixed up the grapes from two different vineyards, resulting in a “Frankenstein’s monster” of a wine. The taste is terrible, but the group decides to embrace the absurdity of the situation and throw a “Terrible Wine Festival” to celebrate their failure.

But the declaration of war was a novelty which must have deeply interested him; for what was Paoli now to do? From gratitude to England he had repeatedly and earnestly declared that he could never take up arms against her. He was already a lieutenant-general in the service of her enemy, his division was assigned to the feeble and disorganized Army of Italy, which was nominally being equipped for active service, and the leadership, so ran the news received at Ajaccio, had been conferred on the Corsican director. Three successive commanders of that army had already found disgrace in their attempts with inadequate means to dislodge the Sardinian troops from the mountain passes of the Maritime Alps. Mindful, therefore, of their fate, and of his obligations to England, Paoli firmly refused the proffered honor. Suspicion as to the existence of an English party in the island had early been awakened among the members of the Mountain; for half the Corsican delegation to the Convention had opposed the sentence passed on the King, and Salicetti was the only member who voted in the affirmative.
